title: What the homepage has to prove for a manufacturer
metaTitle: What a manufacturer homepage must prove
excerpt: Show the object, how it is made, and a path to sales or a spec. A factory photo with no product fails a buyer who needs confidence.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water, beside a piece on what a manufacturer's first screen has to prove.
caption: Color moving through water, as clear as the object on a first screen should be. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a manufacturer put on the first screen?
faqs.answer: The object, a short account of how it is made, and a way to talk to sales or download a spec. Name the part in the buyer's words and show it at a readable scale. A roof shot and a slogan can wait until those three are visible.

faqs.question: Where should the spec download sit?
faqs.answer: In the first screen, next to the sales path, if the file is real. The document should carry dimensions, materials, finishes, and a revision, not a repeat of the headline. If you gate it, say what the buyer receives and what you will do with the email.

faqs.question: How long should the homepage be?
faqs.answer: Short enough that the object, the process, and the next step stay in view. One proof with a named constraint is enough. Move the plant tour, the trophy wall, and the long origin story off this page.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A manufacturer homepage has one job for a buyer who needs specs and confidence: show the object, show how it is made, and offer a way to talk to sales or download a spec. A wide shot of the building, a row of hard hats, and the word quality do not tell an engineer whether the part will match a drawing.

Write the page in that order. The object comes first. The process comes second. The next step comes third. Supporting proof can follow. A factory cliché with no product fails this buyer before the second sentence.

## The object in the first screen

Name the thing in the buyer's words. Housings, castings, labels, benches, garments, boards. The noun they would type into a supplier search belongs in the first line. A headline that says precision manufacturing solutions spends the only line they may read on a category that could be anyone.

Put a photograph of that object where it can be judged. Scale helps. A hand, a known fastener, or a printed dimension gives the picture a size. A floating render on a gray field asks the buyer to trust you before you have shown a part. If you make several families, lead with the one that should generate the next year of inquiries, and list the others as plain links.

The first screen also holds the action. Talk to sales, or download a spec. One of those can be the button. The other can be a text link beside it. A buyer on a plant floor will not scroll through a brand film to find a PDF.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is blunt about the opening. Users often leave within 10–20 seconds. A page that wants more of their time has to communicate its value within about 10 seconds. On this page, that value is the object and the path to a spec. The company story can wait until those are visible.

## How it is made, in a sequence someone owns

Process is the second proof, and it should be short enough to check. Four steps cover most shops. Material in. The operation that defines the part. The inspection. The pack and ship. Name the operations you actually run. If a finish, a weld, a sterilization step, or a calibration is the reason a buyer would switch suppliers, that step gets the sentence. The others can stay on one line.

Put a name on the sequence. A process with no owner reads as a brochure. "Final inspection is signed off in metrology" is more useful than "we take quality seriously." If the work moves between buildings or partners, say so. A buyer who needs confidence is trying to picture the handoff, especially when a drawing leaves their office and comes back as a part.

Lead time and minimums belong near the process when they are stable. When they change with the drawing, say that quotes start from the file. State the rule. A page that hides both feels like it is saving the real answer for a sales call the buyer has not decided to make.

Skip the factory tour. A drone pass over the roof, a spark shower with no part in frame, and a lobby photograph reassure the team that the company looks large. They do not help a person who arrived with a tolerance in mind. One labeled photograph of the cell, the fixture, or the bench does more than a gallery of the site.

## Sales or a spec, with the consequence written down

The next step has to say what happens. "Contact us" is a label, and it is a weak one. "Send a drawing" is a step. "Download the spec sheet" is a step. Pick the action your best buyers already take, and write the consequence under the button.

A spec should be a real file. Dimensions, materials, finishes, what is standard, what is made to order, the revision date. A PDF that repeats the homepage headline is a brochure with a download icon. If the file is public, link it in the first screen. If you gate it, say what the buyer receives and what you will do with the email. A gate in front of a thin file trains people to bounce.

A sales path should name the reply. Who reads the message, what they need from the buyer, and what they send back. A drawing, an annual volume, a material, and a date are a fair ask. A form that demands a novel, a budget range, and a how-did-you-hear-about-us menu is a way to lose a serious inquiry. Keep the fields to what engineering needs for a first look.

If both doors exist, they should agree. The spec and the sales conversation should describe the same product. A buyer who downloads one range and hears another on the phone will trust neither. When the catalog and the custom work differ, say that on the page, in the buyer's language.

## One proof, with the hard part named

The homepage can carry one proof. Choose a job where the constraint is visible. A difficult material. A tolerance the previous supplier missed. A short run that still had to meet a production finish. Write the constraint, the decision, and the object that left the building. Leave the long version for its own page.

Customer logos help when the buyer would recognize them and you have permission. A row of gray boxes that say trusted by industry leaders is a costume. Certifications help when they are in the first questions a buyer asks. Show the mark and the scope. A badge with no scope is a sticker.

Thomas Bewick, a public Hanabi project, is an editorial site for a heritage craft brand. The transferable lesson is specificity. The object and the making are visible enough that a stranger can tell the work is real. Wabisabi, another public project, holds a calm product world together with subject and crop. A manufacturer can use the same standard. The part, the material, and the step that matters. The building is optional.

## The title, the heading, and the words procurement uses

The visible heading should name the object and the buyer it is for. The browser title can carry a plainer phrase a searcher would type. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that are descriptive and concise, and for a main heading that is clearly the main heading. Use that split. The heading can be specific to the part. The title can name the company and the category without turning the hero into a keyword list.

Write the sentences the way a purchasing manager talks. Material, process, finish, lead time, what you need from them. Adjectives that could sit on any supplier's site should come out in the edit. If a claim is true, replace the adjective with the fact. The machine, the standard, the industry, the inspection method.

Keep the page short enough that the three jobs stay in view. The same Nielsen Norman Group article notes that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they visit. A long homepage that performs taste will bury the spec. A shorter page that tells the truth keeps the object, the sequence, and the next step where a hurried buyer can use them.

## Load, motion, and the phone

The product photograph is often the largest thing on the screen. Give it a reserved space so the heading stays still when the file arrives. Compress it. A slow hero of the factory exterior spends the first seconds on the wrong subject. If you use motion, show the object being made, and keep a static frame for people who prefer reduced motion. The path to the spec has to be there either way.

Design the narrow screen while you design the wide one. On a phone, the object, one line about how it is made, and the action still have to fit. A composition that only works on a desktop monitor will push the spec below a cinematic crop. Buyers forward these pages from job sites and from trains. The phone visit is a real visit.

Hanabi designs and builds pages like this in Next.js, with the words in the repository and the spec as a real file someone can replace. The point of the stack is ordinary and useful. The headline can change. The PDF can change. The page still shows one object, one process, and one next step. After delivery, brand files and project notes can live in the client portal so the spec and the photographs do not end as attachments in a thread.

## What to bring to the first working session

Bring one product family, one process you are willing to show, and the file a good buyer would download. If the photograph does not exist, bring the part and a decision about what must be in frame. A shot list is more useful than a stock image chosen to fill a box. If sales and engineering disagree about the next step, settle it before the layout starts. The page cannot offer a gated brochure and a one-field drawing upload and still read as a single offer.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) when you want to see whether the first screen can carry the object, the making, and a real next step. Bring the page you have, or the photograph and the spec if the page is still a document.

The buyer who accepts the object will ask what it costs, or at least what shape the cost takes. Read [a pricing page for a manufacturer](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-manufacturer) next, because the shape of the price has to stay visible or a clear homepage still loses the inquiry.
